subject: Cloud Computing
title: On-Premises vs. Cloud
description: A fast breakdown of On-Premises vs. Cloud for builders.

hook.text: Before the cloud, companies ran everything themselves: servers, networks, storage, software, security.

buildup.text: On-premises means you own and control every layer. Total freedom — and total responsibility.

discovery.text: Cloud offloads layers. IaaS removes hardware worries. PaaS removes OS worries. SaaS removes all of them.

twist.text: Some companies moved to cloud, then moved back. Regulation, cost, or latency drove them home.

climax.text: On-prem isn't dead. It's a deliberate choice for organizations with the resources to do it right.

punchline.text: Cloud isn't always better. Sometimes you want your own kitchen.

quiz.question: Why do some companies return to on-premises after moving to cloud?
options: Regulatory requirements, cost control, or latency needs
Cloud providers force all customers to leave after five years
On-premises servers are always faster than cloud servers

details.summary: On-premises infrastructure gives organizations full control over hardware and data but requires capital investment, facility management, and dedicated staff. Cloud trades some control for flexibility, speed, and the elimination of physical infrastructure responsibility.
details.whyItMatters: The on-premises vs cloud decision affects capital allocation, staffing, agility, and security posture. Making the right choice for each workload drives business outcomes.
takeaways: On-premises offers full control but requires capital investment
Cloud offers flexibility and speed with operational expense
Most enterprises use a hybrid of both approaches

faq.question: Is cloud always cheaper than on-premises?
faq.answer: Not always. For steady-state, high-utilization workloads running 24/7, on-premises can be cheaper over 3 to 5 years. Cloud excels for variable workloads, rapid scaling needs, and when avoiding upfront capital expenditure matters more than minimizing long-run unit cost.

faq.question: Why do some companies move back from cloud?
faq.answer: Cloud repatriation happens when cloud costs exceed expectations, workloads have predictable steady-state demand, or regulatory requirements favor owned infrastructure. Companies like Basecamp have publicly moved workloads back on-premises citing cost savings.
